articles.title_orig: At Least 4 Dead After Explosion in Athens Tourist District
articles.title_zh: At Least 4 Dead After Explosion in Athens Tourist District
articles.content_orig:
The explosion happened in the central Plaka district of the Greek capital
At least two people have died, with a British national among four more missing, after an explosion destroyed a building housing a holiday rental property in the historic centre of Athens.
The blast happened in the Plaka area of the Greek capital, a neighbourhood close to tourist sites such as the Acropolis.
An American man and woman have died, with two more US tourists missing, AFP news agency reported citing local officials. A Greek national and UK national who lived in the building are also said to be missing.
Pictures from the scene showed emergency service workers searching through rubble, with a gas leak the suspected cause of the blast.
The body of a woman was found on Saturday morning, with a Greek fire official later telling reporters the body of a man had also been found.
The tourists were confirmed to be missing when they did not arrive for their flight at Athens airport, Reuters news agency reported citing local police.
Athens Mayor Haris Doukas said: "We are talking about an incredible disaster."
The three-storey building completely collapsed due to the force of the blast, with neighbouring buildings damaged and debris scattered across the road.
Local media reported people were injured by material scattered across nearby streets and some buildings needed to be evacuated.
Excavators and thermal imaging cameras have been used at the scene to search for survivors.
The explosion happened on a small road situated between two of Athens' most visited sites - the Acropolis and the Temple of Olympian Zeus.
A UK Foreign Office spokesperson said: "We are aware of a suspected explosion in Athens and are in touch with the local authorities."

articles.title_orig: Roads flood in New Jersey, inundate some homes, as first major signs of nor'easter take shape
articles.title_zh: Roads flood in New Jersey, inundate some homes, as first major signs of nor'easter take shape
articles.content_orig:
Surf breaks along the rocky coastline, with the twin lighthouses of Thatcher Island visible in the distance, during the early stages of a nor'easter Friday, Sept. 25, 2026, in Gloucester, Mass. Robert F. Bukaty/FR172387 AP Photo hide caption
Thousands were without power on the U.S. East Coast on Friday night as roads flooded in some coastal New Jersey communities, the first major signs of a powerful nor'easter expected to create dangerous conditions through the weekend.
Tens of millions of people are in the path of the storm already beginning to lash the region with strong winds and rain as it braces for much more. Dangerous flooding is expected along the Mid-Atlantic coast, particularly near New Jersey and Delaware, according to the National Weather Service.
In the coastal New Jersey borough of Surf City, water, with waves rippling along its surface, flooded the streets, inundating some homes. About 34 miles (54.7 kilometers) up the coast in the borough of Manasquan, where some roads were also flooding, Mayor Mike Mangan said he expected "a lot of water in the streets for a long time." A voluntary evacuation had been issued earlier in some low-lying areas of the community.
Concerts were canceled, along with dozens of flights going into airports in Boston, Nantucket and Martha's Vineyard on Friday and Saturday. Several airlines were offering to waive some change or cancellation fees for some East Coast flights through the weekend.
Brian Kelly, the mayor of the tiny New Jersey beach community Sea Bright, said the borough is bracing for winds up to 50 mph (80 kph) and flooding that could reach up to 6 feet (1.8 meters) on some streets. Officials expect the flooding to start Saturday and worsen by midday.
"It's going to be worse than average. We do have probably one or two flooding events a year, sometimes more, sometimes less, but I think this one will be closer to an Irene-scale flooding event," Kelly said, referencing the 2011 storm that caused major flooding in the Northeast. "I hope I'm wrong, but that's my gut feeling."
Kelly hopes hundreds of residents living in low-lying areas will consider evacuating. He said the town will open its recreation center for evacuees.
Peak wind gusts could approach 60 to 65 mph (97 to 105 kph) on Cape Cod, Martha's Vineyard and Nantucket on Friday night and Saturday, compared with about 50 to 55 mph (80 to 89 kph) around Boston and 35 to 40 mph (56 to 64 kph) farther inland, according to Matthew Belk, a meteorologist with NWS in Norton, Massachusetts.
"It's definitely going to be a case of the closer to the coast you are, the more impacts from the storm you're likely to see," Belk said.
Belk said nor'easters are not unusual as New England moves into fall, but one concern this early in the season is that leaves remain on the trees, creating more wind resistance. That could increase the risk of downed limbs, which in turn can cause power outages and leave debris in roads, he said.
Along the Atlantic coasts of New Jersey and Delaware, wind gusts could reach 60 mph (96.6 kph), according to NWS. In southeastern Connecticut and eastern Long Island, New York, gusts could get almost as high, potentially downing tree limbs and power lines.
More than 200 flights to and from airports in Boston, Nantucket, Martha's Vineyard and New York had been canceled Friday, and more cancellations were already in place for Saturday.
Meanwhile, the Red Sox announced their weekend series against the Chicago Cubs would be adjusted. The team moved the Sunday afternoon game to Friday to create a split doubleheader. Separately, Ed Sheeran announced that his high-profile Friday and Saturday shows at Gillette Stadium in Foxborough, Massachusetts, would be canceled due to the storm.
The public ferry service connecting Cape Cod with the islands of Nantucket and Martha's Vineyard was experiencing widespread cancellations Friday due to strong winds and choppy water.
In Rhode Island, ferries were also canceled for Block Island. The disrupted ferry service was expected to also spill into Saturday.
For people who regularly travel to and from the islands, the possibility of getting stuck on one side or the other is "part of life," said Sean Driscoll, a spokesperson for the Woods Hole, Martha's Vineyard and Nantucket Steamship Authority. Most people have backup plans in place for when boats are canceled.
"It's a nuisance, but you know, we know what to do with this kind of stuff at this point," he said. "This is not out of the realm of ordinary."
Ashley Destino of Gloucester, a coastal city in northern Massachusetts, enjoyed a stroll along the beach with her two young children before preparing to hunker down at home during the storm.
"We came to the beach on Friday afternoon because we knew we were going to be inside all weekend," said Destino, who has Legos and arts and crafts activities prepared to entertain her two children, ages 7 and 4.
She also prepared by securing her boat with additional lines, and her husband pulled out a generator in case the electricity goes out.

articles.title_orig: Man City charges: Premier League clubs seeking legal advice amid expected guilty verdicts - sources
articles.title_zh: Man City charges: Premier League clubs seeking legal advice amid expected guilty verdicts - sources
articles.content_orig:
By MIKE KEEGAN, CHIEF SPORTS REPORTER
Published: 16:09 EDT, 25 September 2026 | Updated: 04:25 EDT, 26 September 2026
Manchester City have been found guilty of the vast majority of their rule-break charges concerning the Premier League’s financial regulations.
The competition accused the club of widespread financial cheating over an era of sustained success – with an independent panel hearing concluding in 2024.
The long-awaited verdict has now been reached with the belief it is a victory for the Premier League, despite Man City having strenuously denied the charges.
The verdict could lead to a variety of punishments including huge points deductions, financial penalties, and even relegation.
Daily Mail Sport's Mike Keegan provides answers to the key questions, including the next steps, Man City's expected appeal and how serious the punishment could be.
Manchester City have been found guilty of the vast majority of their 115 Premier League rule-break charges
This cannot be viewed as anything other than an overwhelming victory for the Premier League .
To see Manchester City found guilty of the ‘vast majority’ of the 115 charges is an outcome that Richard Masters will no doubt see as vindication for what has been a costly, long-running legal battle in which the stakes were incredibly high.
It is safe to assume that had the tables turned the other way, the chief executive would have been in P45 territory.
More important than that, those who City feel were the key protagonists, the so-called ‘Red Cartel’, will also feel vindication.
To put it simply, Manchester City have been found guilty of cheating their way to success between 2009 and 2018, a period when they dominated English football.
The verdict cannot be viewed as anything other than an overwhelming victory for the Premier League and its chief executive Richard Masters
There has been no statement from the Premier League, while City’s only says that the process remains ongoing and is subject to strict confidentiality.
What is clear is that City will appeal. What is not clear is whether the sanction will drop before any appeal.
Take your pick. Hefty points deductions, potential relegation and transfer bans are all on the table. Rule W51 in the Premier League handbook states ambiguously that ‘such other penalty as it shall think fit’ is an option.
There is, however, a scepticism among some, based on a lack of noise from many of the other clubs and the lenient punishment recently handed to Chelsea that whatever penalty lands will not see City stripped of titles or relegated. ‘They’ll get a slap on the wrist and ordered to pay legal costs and not much else,’ one exec predicted.
The verdict could lead to a variety of punishments including huge points deductions, financial penalties, and even relegation
In all likelihood City will appeal and recent cases tell us that they tend to be dealt with expeditiously.
An appeal board would be set up, appointed by the chair of the panel and, again, featuring three people. Some feel that this would be an exercise in the Premier League marking its own homework.
At this early stage, it is worth an assumption that City could argue the panel was not impartial. The bad news for them, however, is that this is a high bar to clear.
Unlike City’s case with UEFA, it cannot go to the Court of Arbitration for Sport (who overturned UEFA’s findings).
Last year, in a move believed to have been instigated by former Arsenal chief executive Tim Lewis, the Gunners, Tottenham Hotspur, Liverpool and Manchester United served legal notices reserving their right to take action.
Should the verdict stand, they will then seek damages for a wide variety of issues. The most costly claims are likely to come from those who say they missed out on Champions League qualification during the period in question thanks to City’s law breaking. But the scope would not end there.
Clubs could also, for example, argue that as a result of the breaches they were unable to sign a calibre of player that would have allowed them to be more successful on the field. Some believe £200m would not be out of the question, but that remains to be seen.
Ex-Arsenal chief executive is understood to have instigated a move last year that saw the Gunners, Tottenham, Liverpool and Man United served legal notices reserving their right to take action
WHAT ABOUT THE INDEPENDENT FOOTBALL REGULATOR?
Perhaps unsurprisingly, the Regulator declined to comment when contacted by Daily Mail Sport. However, David Kogan will be well aware of the situation.
The IFR was brought in for a variety of reasons, not least to ensure that those owning the nation’s football clubs were fit and proper to do so. The IFR would have the power to force City’s owners to sell, but such a scenario is viewed as unlikely.
DIDN’T CITY TRIUMPH OVER THE PREMIER LEAGUE RECENTLY ON SPONSORSHIP RULES?
They did, with three senior judges deeming the rules unlawful. As a result, a series of amendments were made. City again launched a legal challenge, but surprisingly came to an agreement with the Premier League in September. Those cases, however, were always separate to the 115, as it became known.

articles.content_orig:
Tehran awaits official response to plan, but US president is said to expect renewed strikes after midterms
Iran is ⁠awaiting an official US response to its proposal to reopen the strait of Hormuz and end fighting in the Middle East war as Donald Trump was reported to have rejected the deal.
Iran raised the diplomatic initiative at the UN general assembly in New York, saying it had been transmitted ⁠to the Americans via Qatari mediators and could ⁠reopen the strategic waterway and put an end ​to hostilities in the region within seven days.
But the US president is sceptical and has told his staff that he sees a renewed bombing campaign as likely after the November US midterm elections, the Wall Street Journal reported, citing unnamed US officials.
Earlier, a US official had ⁠said discussions with Iran through mediators were “positive and constructive”.
Iran has offered to reopen the strait of Hormuz and resume talks on its nuclear programme in seven days if the US lifted its naval blockade of Iranian ports, waived sanctions on Iranian oil sales and observed a ceasefire that would include Lebanon.
The Iranian foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, detailed the proposal to reporters outside the UN security council on Friday, saying the country would also restart stalled talks with the US on Iran’s nuclear programme. “The seven-day timeline will start as soon as the United States accepts this plan,” he said.
Araghchi said the initial steps would take about four to five days to complete, and the strait would be open on the sixth day. “And on day seven, the talks with the US will be started for the final deal on mutually agreed subjects,” he said, referring to the nuclear programme.
“If there is seriousness on the US side to ⁠come to a deal and reopen the strait of Hormuz, everything is now prepared,” Araqchi said.
The Iranians also engaged their Saudi rivals regarding the strait, underscoring the stakes of a seven-month-old conflict that has disrupted oil flows through one of the world’s most critical shipping lanes and taken a toll on the global economy.
Iran’s president, Masoud Pezeshkian, in an interview with the CBS show Face the Nation, said Tehran was ready for talks on its nuclear programme and other issues, but would not accept “bullying or coercion”.
“Iran is not seeking war, but will defend itself against pressure, threats and attacks,” Pezeshkian said, adding that it had already agreed that “we’re not supposed to develop nuclear weapons“.
Previous attempts at diplomacy have failed ‌to end the war, which began on 28 February with US and Israeli attacks.
Since then the war has alternated between pauses and renewed strikes, killing thousands while degrading Iran’s conventional forces and damaging its already ailing economy.
Trump has previously said he was in no rush to reach a deal, even as high oil prices fuel inflation. On the Iranian side, there are questions as to whether the hardliners who dominate the security forces would accept compromises championed by moderates such as Pezeshkian.
Diplomatic efforts surrounding the UN general assembly underscored the global stakes in the conflict, which has disrupted oil flows through one of the world’s most critical shipping lanes and drawn in regional and world powers.
Early on Saturday, Yemen’s ⁠Saudi-led ⁠coalition said ⁠it ​intercepted ‌two ‌drones ‌launched by the Iran-backed ‌Houthis towards ​the ⁠Saudi ​capital, Riyadh.
Iranian-aligned militias in Iraq have been blamed for a pipeline attack that temporarily took more Saudi oil off the market. All the while, Iranian-backed Hezbollah has been engaged with Israeli forces in Lebanon.

articles.title_orig: China, US to open AI ‘communication channel’ after summit, White House says
articles.title_zh: China, US to open AI ‘communication channel’ after summit, White House says
articles.content_orig:
The United States and China have agreed to establish a “communication channel” for artificial intelligence (AI) incidents, the White House said after a summit in Washington, DC.
US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping discussed matters ranging from AI and trade to the stalled war in Iran during a three-day state visit, and confirmed that they would meet for a third and fourth time this year at international summits in China and the US.
The White House said on Friday that the nations agreed to establish a “bilateral communication channel” for AI incidents. There was no immediate comment from Beijing on the White House statement.
The announcement came after a summit short on breakthroughs that was dominated by ceremony, according to Al Jazeera’s Alan Fisher, reporting from the White House.
“There was a lot of ceremony and a lot of pomp. In fact, there was a lot more pomp than progress,” Fisher said. The two sides agreed to extend a trade truce due to expire in November, pushing the deadline to January “to give both sides the chance to talk”.
Trump said the visit had strengthened his personal rapport with Xi, which he said would benefit the US in the long run.
“We’ve had a tremendous visit from two spectacular people, and we really enjoyed it, and I think we’ve made tremendous strides,” Trump said. “We’ve made great strides, very positive for both countries.”
Calling on both nations to pursue “a healthy competition” that acts as “a race of catching up with one another, not a wrestle in which one either wins or loses”, President Xi stated that as “leading nations in artificial intelligence”, the two powers share “the capability and responsibility to develop and manage AI for good”.
Fisher reported that Xi used the summit to press specific aims, seeking assurance that China would be “treated more fairly” in future dealings and laying out guidelines he wants to shape upcoming talks between the two countries.
Xinhua reported Xi also urged Trump to “handle the Taiwan issue prudently” along with discussions on the Middle East, Ukraine, and the Korean Peninsula.
On trade, the White House said China agreed to import at least 10 million metric tonnes of US coal in 2027-2028, with more favourable tariffs on $30bn of “non-sensitive goods” each way. Two pandas are also set to arrive at a US zoo.
The visit featured a state banquet, a military parade and a tour of the National Archives, where the leaders viewed the Declaration of Independence and Constitution. Trump noted the US “goes 250 years; theirs goes 6,000 years”.
The two leaders will meet again at the APEC summit in Shenzhen in November and the G20 in Miami in December.
Fisher said the continuation of dialogue was “perhaps the biggest deliverable for both sides”.

articles.title_zh: US got pandas from China. Trump needs a lot more than that | Opinion
articles.content_orig:
While US president hailed visit as ‘great’, almost nothing of substance was achieved on resolving thorny issues
Key takeaways from the Trump-Xi summit in Washington
If the Beijing meeting between Donald Trump and Xi Jinping in May was the “ stalemate summit ”, the second round of talks between the presidents of the US and China this week seemed to give up entirely on the idea of breakthroughs.
Instead, it was described as a celebration of “ diplotainment ” rather than diplomacy, where pomp prevailed over progress and where one of the main outcomes was the news that two giant pandas would soon be sent from China to Atlanta zoo.
Trump rolled out the red carpet for Xi’s arrival on Wednesday and broke with decades of precedent to meet the Chinese leader at Joint Base Andrews. Thus began a three-day state visit that involved a tour of Trump’s new helipad and the Marine One helicopter, and a 90-minute meeting that Trump described as “great” and that revealed, according to Trump, that Xi “has great interest in granite”.
“The biggest takeaway is that Trump has been displaying an extraordinary degree of deference to Xi Jinping,” said Julian Gewirtz, who served as a senior China official in the Biden administration.
But what of actual substance? Expectations going into the summit were low. But the outcomes somehow still fell short.
One of the biggest issues in the US-China relationship is trade. Last year, as Trump unveiled successive rounds of tariffs on Chinese goods, the White House accused China of unfair practices that it said contributed to the loss of 3.7m US jobs and inflated the trade deficit. The tariffs were supposed to suppress the volume of Chinese imports to the US and put pressure on China.
To some degree, they worked. The US trade deficit with China in 2025 fell to $200bn, down from nearly $300bn in 2024. But experts have noted that some of this shortfall is made up for by Chinese goods being shipped to the US via third countries, a trend underlined by the fact that China’s trade surplus surpassed a record $1tn last year.
With the US and China accounting for 43% of global GDP, their trade war has far-reaching implications for the world economy. So it was a relief not just to Beijing and to US consumers when the two countries agreed a temporary truce in Busan last year.
That truce is due to expire in November. China, where the economy is heavily reliant on exports, was reported to be pushing for the truce to be extended until the end of Trump’s term, in January 2029.
On Thursday, it was revealed that Xi’s first state visit to the US in more than a decade had resulted in a mere two-month extension. That reflects “the lack of preparation for this summit beyond the pomp and circumstance”, said Neil Thomas, a senior fellow at the Asia Society.
William Yang, a senior analyst at the International Crisis Group, said: “This summit largely achieved symbolism and ritualism over substance. That is very clear.” The short extension “reflects the level of fundamental differences that still exist between the two countries over a variety of issues”.
China’s most powerful response to Trump’s tariffs was the decision to block the export of rare earths, critical minerals vital to US manufacturing and military supply chains. That seemed to skewer Trump’s leverage over China.
Gewirtz said: “Beijing’s retaliation … seems to have had a profound effect on [Trump] and his administration’s willingness to take risks vis-a-vis China.”
Apart from the trade war agreement, the summit failed to achieve any meaningful progress on thorny issues in the US-China relationship such as artificial intelligence, Taiwan, the wars in Iran and Ukraine, and human rights.
On Taiwan, which Beijing considers to be the most important issue in the relationship, Xi put pressure on Trump to weaken the US’s support for the self-governing island that China claims as its own. According to the Chinese readout of the Xi-Trump meeting, Xi told Trump he hoped “the US side will adhere to the correct position of opposing Taiwan independence”.
For the US to state that it “opposes” Taiwanese independence would be a rhetorical shift from the current position of “does not support” such a claim, and would be a move welcomed by Beijing. Trump has not yet commented on whether he agreed to such a statement. But it does seem he is no closer to approving a $14bn arms sale package for Taiwan, a sale that Beijing would like to see disappear completely.
On Thursday, US Senate Democrats lambasted Trump for opting for “pageantry over purpose” and for failing to deliver agreements on “the economic and security issues that will shape America’s future”. Trump ignored recent warnings about the dangers posed by AI, writing on social media on Thursday: “I want ​to leave it exactly where it is,” adding: “That is China’s position also.”
For China, the lack of big news from the visit is a win in itself. “The summit went excellently from the Chinese perspective,” Thomas said. Xi “got a huge amount of respect from the American president, the full state visit treatment [and] really great images beaming back to China of the Chinese and the American presidents interacting as peers on the global stage, without having to make any meaningful concessions or compromises.”

articles.content_orig:
By TOM LEONARD, US CORRESPONDENT
Published: 18:04 EDT, 25 September 2026 | Updated: 03:38 EDT, 26 September 2026
Woke Is Dead ran the title of a bestselling book by the broadcaster Piers Morgan last year.
Many obituaries have been written for the social contagion that arguably reached its apex during the pandemic, when millions were locked in their houses, scrolling social media and getting increasingly furious about Black Lives Matter and other assorted 'injustices'.
Well, if woke really is dead, no one told the owners of the Last Ditch Bar in Greenfield, Massachusetts . The scruffy establishment, which caters chiefly to lesbians, could be the most woke institution left on Planet Earth.
This week, it has found itself embroiled in a controversy that, as the colloquialism goes, has 'broken the internet'.
The Boston Globe – the first newspaper to report the story – is set to receive the biggest subscription boost in its history over the viral article, and the initial tweet about the story has been viewed more than 30 million times.
The row has sparked astonishment from figures such as the Republican Texas Senator Ted Cruz , as well as incredulity even from The Guardian, plus conservative Fox News and the New York Post.
One online pundit accurately summed up the general public's response, calling the situation 'intergalactic woke batcrapitude'.
In particular, the bizarre episode has revealed how a baffling number of Left-wingers, rather like those Japanese soldiers in the jungles of Guam who believed they were still fighting the Second World War long after it had ended, have not updated their worldview in six long years.
If woke really is dead, no one told the owners of the Last Ditch Bar in Greenfield, Massachusetts (pictured)
Pictured: The 'house rules' of the lesbian venue Last Ditch Bar which sparked a war in Massachusetts after dropping their face mask mandate
The stern 'venue norms' of Last Ditch are plastered over the walls of the basement venue.
'Racism, Misogynoir [racism directed towards black women], Transmisogyny, Ableism, Transphobia, Homophobia, Lesbophobia, and any other discrimination will not be tolerated,' declares one of these house rules.
'No one is permitted to touch anyone, in any way, without getting express, verbal consent,' ran another – an injunction that even includes touching patrons' 'assistive devices' such as wheelchairs, canes and hearing aids, should they have any.
A third rule proclaims: 'Nobody will be barred from entry due to lack of funds. Poor and unhoused [sic] people are welcome in the space.'
But it was the requirement that every punter wear a 'well-fitted KN-95 respirator mask (or better) at all times' that is perhaps the most surprising.
These are the exceptionally cumbersome and uncomfortable masks designed to prevent the spread of respiratory viruses such as Covid-19 .
The bar, which calls the masks 'safety belts for the face', specified that the buzz-killing accessories are 'required when not actively taking a sip of your drink or taking a bite of a snack. Lower, sip, and lift!'
Anyone who fell foul of this stricture would expect to be asked to leave, although they might first be 'provided with an opportunity to engage in an accountability process'.
The Last Ditch, then, didn't exactly scream 'fun night out'. The management's propensity for making cringingly self-righteous statements on various matters probably didn't help.
Last September, for example, it announced it was banning all law enforcement from the premises after a police officer pursuing two drugs suspects had briefly come into the bar looking for them.
'We reserve the right to refuse entry and service to the pigs in all their forms,' proclaimed the bar on social media, accompanying this act of rebel bravado with a picture of a person throwing a Molotov cocktail.
Perhaps not surprisingly, the bar, which only opened last year, swiftly began running into financial difficulties.
The Last Ditch's founders – a trio of 20-something housemates that included a drag performer who uses 'it/its' pronouns and another who is now training to become a professional clown, both of whom have since left – soon found themselves unable to meet their costs.
Facing closure, the remaining owner, Jackie Matellian, decided to relax the mandatory mask policy for just one night per week.
A month ago, the bar announced this momentous change in a rainbow-coloured Instagram post to its 11,300 followers, saying: 'It is with love we inform our immunocompromised disabled divas we will be opening Saturday nights as "mask optional"...
'Our mission is to also make the space work for everyone and everything radical, sometimes that's being wild!'
The venue owners required every punter to wear a 'well-fitted KN-95 respirator mask (or better) at all times'
The backlash was immediate, ferocious and highly revealing. No matter that Greenfield hasn't reported any Covid cases for months, or that the pandemic was officially declared over by the World Health Organisation in 2023. All hell broke loose.
Hundreds of angry comments flooded the bar's social media accounts, with many calling for a boycott and others threatening violence. The owners were branded 'eugenicists' intent on murdering the sick.
One protester (who says she is raising her child, named Cloud, to be 'gender neutral') called for the bar to be burnt to the ground, writing: 'I hope your venue gets firebombed for robbing my fellow immunocompromised people of their Saturday plans just to scrape extra revenue from ablists [sic].'
Another accused the bar's management of trying to 'kill disabled people in the name of your own leisure and convenience'.
'Just say you're being complicit in a mass disabling event and get it over with,' one said. 'What is truly being WILD is announcing a change of this magnitude in such a cavalier, callous fashion,' screeched another.
Stunned at the outcry, which came mainly from the bar's patrons rather than armchair progressives thousands of miles away, Last Ditch posted a craven apology two days later reminiscent of something out of a Soviet show trial.
'We are sorry for our passive and dismissive tone of our change to the norms and schedule impacting the most intersectional of us,' grovelled the management. 'We understand everyone faces different intersections [sic] and we are always working to consider all needs fully.'
But this apology only sparked more pious complaints: Because they hadn't written the statement in 'alternative text' [additional written description suitable for the visually impaired], they were met with renewed accusations of 'ableism'.
When the bar's management held its regular 'community meeting' earlier this month to address the controversy, the crisis became a farce.
The session – in which heavily masked participants sat in a circle on a floor around a stripper pole – started with a 'calm breathing exercise' to quell passions.
However, the three-and-a-half hour summit was swiftly hijacked by the black founder of another 'Covid-conscious collective' in western Massachusetts, who lambasted the white therapist running the meeting.
Others attending via Zoom suggested this therapist was an agent of the state who could have them hospitalised, calling her presence 'wildly unsafe'.
When the bar's only remaining owner burst into tears after revealing that its financial problems had left her living in her car, owing the landlord nearly £3,000 and struggling to pay off the £38,000 loan she had taken out to launch the business, she was accused of shedding 'WHITE THEY/THEM TEARS'.
As the extraordinary tale spread like a firestorm across the internet, the initial 442 messages condemning the relaxing of the mask strictures on Last Ditch's Instagram page were swamped by thousands of others bemoaning the sheer levels of wokery remaining on the Left and expressing astonishment that a mask rule was ever thought necessary in the first place.

articles.title_zh: The damage of the Manchester City verdict runs deep. An era of Premier League history is tainted - The Athletic
articles.content_orig:
By MICHAEL PAVITT, SPORTS REPORTER
Published: 16:35 EDT, 25 September 2026 | Updated: 03:14 EDT, 26 September 2026
Former Manchester City captain Rodri insists he 'believes in the club' and their success cannot be taken away after they were found guilty of the vast majority of their Premier League rule break charges.
Rodri, whose seven-year spell at Man City ended in the summer when he moved to Barcelona , became the first individual associated with the club to speak following the bombshell news on Friday.
Daily Mail Sport understands Man City were found guilty of the vast majority of their 115 charges by an independent panel.
The verdict could lead to a variety of punishments including huge points deductions, financial penalties and even relegation.
Points deductions could even be applied onto previous seasons, raising the chance that City will be stripped of their Premier League titles.
When asked about the verdict ahead of Spain's Nations League match against England on Saturday, Rodri reiterated his belief Man City will be found innocent.
Rodri has insisted Man City's success cannot be taken away from them despite the club being found guilty of the majority their Premier League rule break charges
The former Man City captain insisted he believes in the innocence of the club amid the verdict
The midfielder referenced a previous 2020 decision which saw Man City banned from the Champions League and fined by UEFA for a breach of financial rules, which was later lifted on appeal by the Court of Arbitration for Sport which also reduced the club's fine to £9million.
'We have faced something similar in 2020 if I remember correctly, a similar process, a different accusation but similar process.
‘In the first instance we were found guilty but we believed in the club and the innocence the club maintained, and in the end we ended up being acquitted.
‘I believe in the justice system and I believe in the innocence of the club.’
When asked whether he had been given assurances by the club of their innocence, Rodri added: 'They always tell us the confidence of their innocence and when you look in someone’s eyes and they are talking in that way – and we have the example of 2020 the process was the same and at the end nothing happened – we were very calm in this way.
'We were never a team that was nervous about these kind of things. I am not going to say it is normal but some teams go through these situations and it is part of football today.
'Everyone has to follow the rules and for me that’s great. They always expressed the confidence they never did anything wrong and we believe in that, and that’s the thing.
'We will believe the club. I have been there and I know how they work and how they cooperate.'
Rodri insisted Man City's success was 'deserved' and the result of hard work from the players and staff
Rodri won four Premier League titles, the Champions League, two FA Cups, three Carabao Cups and a FIFA Club World Cup during a glittering spell at Man City under Pep Guardiola.
When asked whether he it hurt that Man City's achievements have been questioned, Rodri insisted the success of the players and staff during that period cannot be taken away.
'For us, the players, it is a different thing. For you guys there are all kinds of opinions but we always tried to think in a positive way,' Rodri said.
'When you live daily in that club and all the people that worked hard all these years to have all the success we have had, not only Pep [Guardiola] and the players, but from the owners to the guys that work daily, what we did they cannot take it out of us.
'It is not something that is paid by money, it is paid with effort and partnership, being shoulder to shoulder every day.
'We had a lot of success over the years and I can tell you that everything was deserved and I am glad I could live one of the best eras in English football.'
Man City are set to appeal the verdict.
A Manchester City spokesperson said: 'The Premier League process remains ongoing, with significant elements to be completed, and subject to strict confidentiality. As such Manchester City FC’s position remains consistent with the Club’s statement of February 2023.
'The Club has diligently respected due process for eight years on the basis that the Premier League Board and Executive would behave as an independent, impartial and fair-minded regulator, free from partisan influence.'
The club have maintained that they are innocent throughout the process and are expected to appeal
Man City, who have always strongly denied wrongdoing, were charged in February 2023 by the Premier League with a hearing concluding in December 2024.
Their statement that February insisted that they were 'surprised' by the charges.
The Premier League accused Man City of multiple breaches of financial rules and of failing to co-operate with a subsequent investigation. The alleged rule breaking was claimed to have taken place over a 14-year period.
A three-man panel was tasked with considering the evidence, with the initial expectation a verdict would have been reached on the case within months. It has since taken three-and-a-half years.
The original 115 charges were extended to a total of 130 after an administration issue in what is the most expensive and wide-ranging case in English football history.
City remained steadfast in maintaining their innocence over more than 115 alleged breaches across eight years, some including the start of the Pep Guardiola era.
The club were accused of failing to report accurate financial information for nine seasons stretching from 2009-10 to 2017-18, as well as failing to provide full details of former manager Roberto Mancini’s pay between 2009-10 and 2012-13.
They were also alleged to have failed to provide full details of money paid to players between 2010-11 and 2015-16 and failing to co-operate with the probe from 2018 to 2023.

articles.title_zh: White House blocks CNN from trip on Air Force One
articles.content_orig:
Outlet had been scheduled to fly with Donald Trump to Tennessee for a college football game, network said Friday
The White House has blocked CNN from traveling aboard Air Force One on Saturday, impeding its TV press pool duties in the latest escalation of the administration’s battle with the news media.
CNN had been scheduled to fly with Donald Trump to Tennessee for a college football game, the network said on Friday . The White House confirmed CNN’s exclusion when it did not list the network on guidance sent to the press corps regarding Trump’s schedule for Saturday.
CNN’s exclusion from Air Force One was first reported by the Washington Post . The White House did not immediately return the Guardian’s request for comment.
The incident comes a week after Trump, a vocal critic of what he deems the “fake news media”, revoked White House access for CNN, MS Now and Politico, citing unfavorable reports about his presidency.
“Media Outlets shouldn’t be able to constantly write or report FICTION and LIES,” Trump wrote then on Truth Social, vowing that similar action would be taken against other outlets.
The extraordinary move prompted swift backlash from the White House press pool, who suspended their video coverage of Trump in protest.
The press pool is a rotating group of journalists charged with covering presidential travel and disseminating written and multimedia reports to news outlets that may not be present at a given White House event. Since the beginning of Trump’s second administration in 2025, the White House has decided which outlets cover the president via the pool each day, a task previously coordinated by the White House Correspondents’ Association.
In a joint statement Monday, the White House television pool said: “The public has a vital interest in receiving accurate, independent information about its government. No administration should restrict a news organization because it objects to its reporting.”
In a subsequent lawsuit , CNN, MS Now and Politico argued the White House ban was a violation of the first amendment.
Meanwhile, the Department of Justice’s attorneys suggested the ban was in the interest of national security, pointing at media reports involving “sensitive” and “classified” information.
The US district judge Timothy Kelly sided with the outlets, ordering the Trump administration to restore their White House access.
CNN, MS Now and Politico’s journalists sought to enter the White House on Thursday morning, but were not granted entry until midday.
Hours later, CNN’s editorial team along with an MS Now reporter were blocked from covering the state dinner commemorating Chinese president Xi Jinping’s visit.

articles.title_orig: Hurricane Nolo expected to bring heavy rain as it skirts Hawaii’s Big Island
articles.title_zh: Hurricane Nolo expected to bring heavy rain as it skirts Hawaii’s Big Island
articles.content_orig:
NAALEHU, Hawaii — Hurricane Nolo is forecast to strengthen into a major hurricane in the Pacific Ocean over the weekend, unleashing intense rain, the possibility of life-threatening flash flooding, and dangerous surf for Hawaii’s Big Island.
Nolo was a Category 2 hurricane with maximum sustained winds of 105 mph when its outer rainbands began hitting Big Island Friday evening, the National Hurricane Center said. Come Saturday, hurricane conditions are possible on the island, especially in areas with steep terrain, the weather service warned.
The storm was about 145 miles south of South Point, the southernmost point of the Big Island, at around 5 p.m. local time, and was moving north-northeast at 3 mph.
This marks the third hurricane in less than two months to whip past Hawaii (following Lala and Lowell ). The active Pacific hurricane season is likely due to a record-setting El Niño — a natural climate pattern characterized by a rise in sea surface temperatures in the eastern Pacific, and spawns more intense and frequent cyclones there.
Tess Kala, a South Point resident who grew up in the area, said the back-to-back storms are a shock to locals.
“Honestly, this is the first like, whoa, what happened? We had a lot of family and friends that have lived here all their lives through generations and never experienced this before,” she said.
On its current path, Nolo will move slowly northward Friday night, but will remain south of Big Island through Saturday. Then, it will turn westward and move away from the island but increase in speed Saturday into Sunday, the hurricane center said.
Nolo’s center will remain well south of the main Hawaiian islands, the National Hurricane Center said. But it is forecast to strengthen into a “major hurricane” — which means Category 3 or higher — this weekend and could intensify further next week, the agency said,
Hawaii Gov. Josh Green said Friday that President Donald Trump approved the state’s request for an emergency declaration for Nolo to provide federal assistance for emergency protective measures across the state.
Mark Peters, a resident of Naalehu in the southern Big Island for seven years, said that the damage from the recent hurricanes has not been forgotten.
“It hurts me when I see friends and neighbors and people of this community that I know, and I just see it in their eyes, I hear it in their voices. We’ve been through a lot down here, and we still got a lot to go,” Peters said.
“We’re just getting started with our recovery. But to have yet another big storm hit us, and potentially even bigger than the last one, it’s difficult,” he said.
While he praised his community for its resilience, he said the people are still in need of basics like food and water, and many are in the process of reconstruction.
“We’re talking years. This is going to be a long recovery,” Peters said Friday.
He recalled driving through Waiohinu in the aftermath of Hurricane Lala and his “eyes getting wide open with all the damage, and the cars and houses moved and not where they’re supposed to be, and Waiohinu Park having buildings in the baseball field.”
Kala, the South Point resident, is preparing for Nolo by “moving everything away from the houses, tying things down, making sure that everything is hosed up and taped up as best as we possibly can.”
Nolo will bring periods of heavy rain that will continue across Big Island and Maui over the weekend, and could trigger life-threatening catastrophic flooding and mudslides, especially in steep terrain across eastern and southern portions of both Big Island and Maui, the hurricane center said.
Nolo is forecast to dump 8 to 12 inches of rain in eastern and southern parts of Big Island, with maximum amounts up to 16 inches. Western portions of Big Island could see one to three inches of rain with maximum amounts of six inches. Meanwhile, Maui could see four to six inches, with maximum amounts of eight inches, the National Hurricane Center said.
The rest of Hawaii will experience lesser rainfall totals but isolated flooding is possible.
Nolo could also bring large and damaging waves along portions of Big Island’s coastline into the weekend.
A hurricane watch and tropical storm warning are in effect for Hawaii County and a tropical storm watch is in effect for Maui County. A hurricane watch means that hurricane conditions are possible within 24-36 hours. A wind advisory has been issued for the rest of the state.
Tropical storm force winds will reach the Big Island on Friday afternoon, with hurricane force winds possible by late evening.
A high surf advisory is in effect for south and east facing shores of Big Island and east facing shores of Maui and Molokai. A high surf advisory was also issued for east facing shores of Niihau, Kauai, and Oahu beginning Friday evening.
Nolo could also spawn tornadoes and large waterspouts over and near Big Island and to the right of the track of the tropical cyclone.
Marlene Lenthang reported from Los Angeles and Ryan Chandler and Shanshan Dong from Naalehu.

articles.title_orig: Roads flood in New Jersey, inundate some homes, as first major signs of nor'easter take shape
articles.title_zh: Roads flood in New Jersey, inundate some homes, as first major signs of nor'easter take shape
articles.content_orig:
Surf breaks along the rocky coastline, with the twin lighthouses of Thatcher Island visible in the distance, during the early stages of a nor'easter Friday, Sept. 25, 2026, in Gloucester, Mass. Robert F. Bukaty/FR172387 AP Photo hide caption
Thousands were without power on the U.S. East Coast on Friday night as roads flooded in some coastal New Jersey communities, the first major signs of a powerful nor'easter expected to create dangerous conditions through the weekend.
Tens of millions of people are in the path of the storm already beginning to lash the region with strong winds and rain as it braces for much more. Dangerous flooding is expected along the Mid-Atlantic coast, particularly near New Jersey and Delaware, according to the National Weather Service.
In the coastal New Jersey borough of Surf City, water, with waves rippling along its surface, flooded the streets, inundating some homes. About 34 miles (54.7 kilometers) up the coast in the borough of Manasquan, where some roads were also flooding, Mayor Mike Mangan said he expected "a lot of water in the streets for a long time." A voluntary evacuation had been issued earlier in some low-lying areas of the community.
Concerts were canceled, along with dozens of flights going into airports in Boston, Nantucket and Martha's Vineyard on Friday and Saturday. Several airlines were offering to waive some change or cancellation fees for some East Coast flights through the weekend.
Brian Kelly, the mayor of the tiny New Jersey beach community Sea Bright, said the borough is bracing for winds up to 50 mph (80 kph) and flooding that could reach up to 6 feet (1.8 meters) on some streets. Officials expect the flooding to start Saturday and worsen by midday.
"It's going to be worse than average. We do have probably one or two flooding events a year, sometimes more, sometimes less, but I think this one will be closer to an Irene-scale flooding event," Kelly said, referencing the 2011 storm that caused major flooding in the Northeast. "I hope I'm wrong, but that's my gut feeling."
Kelly hopes hundreds of residents living in low-lying areas will consider evacuating. He said the town will open its recreation center for evacuees.
Peak wind gusts could approach 60 to 65 mph (97 to 105 kph) on Cape Cod, Martha's Vineyard and Nantucket on Friday night and Saturday, compared with about 50 to 55 mph (80 to 89 kph) around Boston and 35 to 40 mph (56 to 64 kph) farther inland, according to Matthew Belk, a meteorologist with NWS in Norton, Massachusetts.
"It's definitely going to be a case of the closer to the coast you are, the more impacts from the storm you're likely to see," Belk said.
Belk said nor'easters are not unusual as New England moves into fall, but one concern this early in the season is that leaves remain on the trees, creating more wind resistance. That could increase the risk of downed limbs, which in turn can cause power outages and leave debris in roads, he said.
Along the Atlantic coasts of New Jersey and Delaware, wind gusts could reach 60 mph (96.6 kph), according to NWS. In southeastern Connecticut and eastern Long Island, New York, gusts could get almost as high, potentially downing tree limbs and power lines.
More than 200 flights to and from airports in Boston, Nantucket, Martha's Vineyard and New York had been canceled Friday, and more cancellations were already in place for Saturday.
Meanwhile, the Red Sox announced their weekend series against the Chicago Cubs would be adjusted. The team moved the Sunday afternoon game to Friday to create a split doubleheader. Separately, Ed Sheeran announced that his high-profile Friday and Saturday shows at Gillette Stadium in Foxborough, Massachusetts, would be canceled due to the storm.
The public ferry service connecting Cape Cod with the islands of Nantucket and Martha's Vineyard was experiencing widespread cancellations Friday due to strong winds and choppy water.
In Rhode Island, ferries were also canceled for Block Island. The disrupted ferry service was expected to also spill into Saturday.
For people who regularly travel to and from the islands, the possibility of getting stuck on one side or the other is "part of life," said Sean Driscoll, a spokesperson for the Woods Hole, Martha's Vineyard and Nantucket Steamship Authority. Most people have backup plans in place for when boats are canceled.
"It's a nuisance, but you know, we know what to do with this kind of stuff at this point," he said. "This is not out of the realm of ordinary."
Ashley Destino of Gloucester, a coastal city in northern Massachusetts, enjoyed a stroll along the beach with her two young children before preparing to hunker down at home during the storm.
"We came to the beach on Friday afternoon because we knew we were going to be inside all weekend," said Destino, who has Legos and arts and crafts activities prepared to entertain her two children, ages 7 and 4.
She also prepared by securing her boat with additional lines, and her husband pulled out a generator in case the electricity goes out.

articles.title_zh: CNN left off Air Force One for Trump's upcoming trip, White House signals in new media restriction
articles.content_orig:
The motorcade of President Donald Trump departs the White House en route to the National Archives to greet China's President Xi Jinping and his wife Peng Liyuan, Friday, Sept. 25, 2026, in Washington. Jacquelyn Martin/AP hide caption
CNN was replaced by the conservative Real America's Voice News. The news came just after journalists from three news outlets that Trump banned last week from the White House grounds returned to the executive complex with TV cameras, laptops and microphones in hand. Trump is scheduled travel to Knoxville, Tennessee, and attend a college football game between Tennessee and Texas.
The White House signaled Friday night that CNN would be left off Air Force One for President Donald Trump's Saturday trip, the latest media restriction from the administration in an ongoing dispute with First Amendment implications.
The news organization was replaced by Real America's Voice News, a conservative network, for the president's trip to Knoxville, Tennessee, according to White House guidance. Trump is scheduled to attend a college football game between the University of Tennessee and the University of Texas at midday Saturday.
The news came just after journalists from CNN, along with MS NOW and Politico, which Trump banned last week from the White House grounds, returned to the executive complex with TV cameras in hand after a judge handed the organizations a reprieve.
U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly temporarily struck down the ban in an overnight ruling early Thursday, but his decision addressed "hard passes" to the White House grounds and didn't directly address pool duties.
The temporary order from the judge also said nothing directly about Air Force One.
Theodore Boutrous Jr., the news outlets' attorneys, did not immediately respond to an email and phone call from The Associated Press requesting comment Friday night.
Earlier Friday, on "The Lead with Jake Tapper," Boutrous had said the plaintiffs believe the recent court ruling also covers the issue of pool access.
The White House did not immediately respond to an email from AP requesting additional details on the decision.
For a while during the day, the U.S. network video pool for the White House was back in operation for the first time since Trump banned the three news outlets in an extraordinary showdown over media access.
At noon on CNN, viewers could see Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping touring the National Archives, along with Melania Trump and Peng Liyuan, Xi's wife. The banner along the bottom of the screen read: "Trump and China's Xi Visit National Archives." It was a routine report from a state visit — but for the fact that CNN had not aired live video of Trump in several days.
"As of now, all systems are go," said a person familiar with the pool, speaking on condition of anonymity because of the fluidity of the situation.
The pool consists of five major U.S. broadcast outlets that take turns shooting and sharing video. When the White House banned CNN — which belongs to the pool — from White House grounds, along with MS NOW and Politico, the other four pool providers declined to participate in a show of solidarity.
The spot that was meant for CNN on this flight has long been saved for a member of the U.S. network video pool, which Real America's Voice News is not a part of.
CNN was not commenting directly earlier Friday, referring instead to its editorial coverage. But Brian Stelter, the network's media analyst, posted on X that CNN had a pool assignment at the National Archives event and that the White House had approved the network's credentials.
Throughout his second term, Trump has increasingly targeted media outlets whose coverage irritates him, taking administrative or legal action against several. Early last year he banished AP reporters from White House events because the organization wasn't abiding by his executive order changing the name of the Gulf of Mexico to the "Gulf of America." The AP's guidance says to acknowledge the new name when relevant.
The case is on appeal after a federal district judge ruled in AP's favor.
The press pool was created decades ago by the White House Correspondents' Association, a group of journalists who cover the president, to make sure a rotating roster always travel with the president.
The pool distributes in-person reports and imagery to the broader press corps and is designed to hold the nation's chief executive accountable on behalf of the American public.
The association did not immediately respond to an email requesting comment.

articles.title_orig: We can’t stop the ‘Godzilla’ El Niño – but can we limit its damage?
articles.title_zh: We can’t stop the ‘Godzilla’ El Niño – but can we limit its damage?
articles.content_orig:
The ‘Godzilla’ El Niño is here, and it is already breaking records the world would rather have left unbroken.
Sea surface temperatures in the equatorial Pacific Ocean have already surpassed the highest recorded during any previous El Niño, and the weather phenomenon is still strengthening. Between June 2026 and February 2027, experts estimate the extreme heat associated with it could contribute to 451,000 additional deaths.
The forecast has set off alarm bells among weather agencies, health authorities and governments around the world, including an unprecedented mobilisation by the World Meteorological Organization (WMO) to prepare for the extreme weather ahead.
“El Niño is being supersized before our eyes,” outgoing UN Secretary-General António Guterres said in early September. “The planet is in uncharted waters, and those waters are heating up.”
But even as governments brace for what could be a devastating year of extreme weather, experts say there is still plenty that can be done to limit the damage – both now and in the future.
Records aside, many worry about what an El Niño of this strength could mean for weather around the world in the months ahead.
An El Niño event starts in the Pacific, but its effects can be felt around the world. When waters near the equator become unusually warm, they release heat into the atmosphere, pushing up global temperatures and changing where rain falls.
With ocean temperatures already at record highs, this El Niño could bring more intense heat, drought and heavy rainfall in vulnerable regions and push global temperatures to new highs – earning it the nicknames ‘Godzilla’ and ‘Super’ El Niño.
Some of those effects are already being felt . India has already experienced below-normal monsoon rainfall while southern Africa faces an increased risk of drought.
Even though Europe is unlikely to experience the most severe direct effects, El Niño can influence winter weather, and droughts or failed harvests elsewhere can disrupt supplies of foods imported into Europe.
The threat is already prompting governments to act around the world. This month, California Governor Gavin Newsom preemptively declared a state of emergency to prepare for potential flooding, landslides, coastal erosion and powerful winter storms.
For all the preparations we make, one thing remains unavoidable: El Niño is a natural phenomenon. But even if we can’t prevent it, forecasts give us months to prepare.
“The key is to manage water and prepare for the changes in where and when rainfall occurs,” says Davide Faranda, research director at France’s National Centre for Scientific Research (CNRS) and a lead author for the UN’s Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC).
For example, he explains, governments can store and distribute water more carefully, better control how reservoirs and underground water are used, adjust farming schedules and irrigation practices, and prepare communities for droughts or floods.
The FAO has also offered concrete advice . Farmers, FAO officials say, can reduce losses by changing planting dates, irrigating at cooler times of day, storing water ahead of droughts and taking steps to protect their crops and livestock from extreme heat.
Some governments have stepped up with financial support.
The UK has pledged up to £15 million (€17 million) to help vulnerable countries prepare for this El Niño. The money will fund measures that range from vaccinating livestock before droughts to reinforcing homes before flooding and providing farmers with cash before harvests fail.
Most El Niño events increase global average temperatures by around 0.2°C. While this is enough to trigger extreme weather conditions across the Global South, it is a fraction of the additional warming caused by climate change.
The burning of fossil fuels has pushed global average surface temperatures by approximately 1.3°C to 1.4°C above pre-industrial levels, paving the way for Europe’s scorching summer that triggered mass droughts and wildfires.
El Niño’s impacts are therefore compounded by an already warming world. It’s why 2025 was the third warmest year on record – hotter than the El Niño year of 2016 – despite the naturally forming cool drag of a La Niña event.
Recent research suggests that climate change is turbocharging El Niño as well. A study published in August found that El Niños are 36 per cent stronger than before the industrial era, a trend researchers linked to human-caused warming.
If climate change is making El Niño stronger, then preparation will only go so far. But Faranda says cutting emissions can make a big difference over the long term.
A hotter planet means more extreme heat, more strain on water supplies and, in some places, more rainfall. Reducing emissions would not stop the natural climate cycle that leads to El Niños, he explains, but it would reduce the human-caused warming that is making those threats more severe.
That means the damage is not entirely beyond our control. “We cannot eliminate El Niño through climate mitigation,” Faranda says, “but we can reduce the extent to which climate change makes its consequences more severe.”

articles.title_orig: TikTok to pay Alabama $100m and limit teenage use in first state settlement
articles.title_zh: TikTok to pay Alabama $100m and limit teenage use in first state settlement
articles.content_orig:
Trial had been set for Monday over claims by Alabama that TikTok misled parents about tools meant to shield children from harmful content
TikTok has agreed to pay Alabama at least $100m and enact time limits and other restrictions for teenage users, avoiding a trial with a settlement that was modelled on Instagram-owner Meta’s recent agreement with US states.
Alabama described it as a “first-in-the-nation settlement” with a state in the sweeping litigation over social media’s affect on teen wellbeing.
A trial had been set to begin on Monday in the southern US state over claims by Alabama that TikTok misled parents about tools meant to shield children from harmful content.
TikTok’s settlement with Alabama mirrors safety provisions agreed by Meta, including a two-hour daily time limit for teens, restricted access from midnight to 6am, and suspending notifications during school hours.
It will also strengthen age verification, ban beauty filters for teenagers, and offer young users a non-personalised content feed.
Attorney general Steve Marshall hailed Friday’s settlement as “a great day for Alabama parents”. He said: “Tonight, they can rest easier knowing real protections are in place to shield their children from the dangers of social media addiction.”
Under the settlement, TikTok will send $100m to Alabama and could possibly pay up to $300m in total if 40 other attorneys general sign similar agreements with the company within a specified timeframe.
Alabama’s suit was the latest in a wave of litigation targeting social media companies across the United States about alleged harm their apps cause young users.
In August, Meta agreed to pay $18bn to settle a sweeping lawsuit brought by US states accusing it of designing Instagram and Facebook to get children addicted.
In addition, the Alabama deal includes a conditional restriction that Meta also agreed to: expanding the night-time shutdown period to 10pm to 7am if other platforms also commit to do the same.
“TikTok’s priority has always been fostering a safe and positive space where people can be creative, discover what they love, and connect with their community,” a company spokesperson told AFP.
“This builds on our commitment and core objective to continually enhance our robust safety tools to protect teens,” the spokesperson added.
More than a dozen other states, including California and New York, still havesuits against TikTok.
The company has previously settled cases against it that were headed for trial, including a Los Angeles lawsuit brought by a young woman and a suit from a Kentucky school district.
Meta, by contrast, has taken its chances in court – with bruising results.
In March, a jury in New Mexico ordered the Facebook and Instagram owner to pay $375m after finding it had misled the public about the safety of its platforms for children.
That same month, a Los Angeles jury found Meta and Google’s YouTube negligent in the case of a 20-year-old woman who said she became hooked on social media as a child, awarding her $6m.
Going to trial would have exposed TikTok to unprecedented public scrutiny of how it handles safety, with company documents and executive testimony potentially aired in open court.
Alabama originally sued TikTok and its Chinese parent company ByteDance in April 2025, alleging the app was engineered to hook young users “just like a sophisticated gambling machine”.
The state later narrowed its case to claims under Alabama’s Deceptive Trade Practices Act, focusing on whether TikTok misrepresented the effectiveness of features such as “Restricted Mode” and “Kids Mode.”
The lawsuit accused TikTok of falsely claiming it limits access to sexual and violent content for young users to have its app rated safe for teens in app stores run by Google, Apple and Microsoft and of misleading users about the Chinese government’s access ‌to US users’ data.
TikTok said it designed its platform with teen safety as a key priority and argued that section 230 of the federal Communications Decency Act shields online platforms from liability for user-generated content.

articles.title_orig: Steph Curry takes a discount, signs 2-year extension with Warriors
articles.title_zh: Steph Curry takes a discount, signs 2-year extension with Warriors
articles.content_orig:
Stephen Curry has agreed to a two-year contract extension worth $116 million that would take him through the 2028-29 season, a person with direct knowledge of the deal told The Associated Press on Friday.
The person spoke on condition of anonymity because the team had not announced the terms of Curry's contract. Curry was eligible to command up to $136 million, so he is giving his team a discount as he backs up his longstanding commitment to finish his career with the Warriors.
Golden State general manager Mike Dunleavy said last month he was optimistic of getting something done with the two-time MVP and NBA career leader in 3-pointers.
"We couldn't be more excited about reaching an agreement with Stephen and extending his historic career with the Warriors," Dunleavy said in a statement. "There has never been a better face to a franchise in professional sports history, both on and off the court, than Stephen Curry with the Warriors. He embodies everything this organization strives to represent through his legendary play on the court, his unique leadership and sacrifice, and his unmatched impact in the community."
The 38-year-old Curry will complete a $62.6 million extension he signed for the 2026-27 season in August 2024, and the new contract takes him through 2029 — his 20th season.
If he plays that 20th year, he would join Dirk Nowitzki of Dallas, the late Kobe Bryant of the Los Angeles Lakers, and Udonis Haslem of Miami as the only players in NBA history to play 20 or more seasons with one franchise.
Curry averaged 26.6 points, 4.7 assists, 3.6 rebounds and 1.1 steals while playing 30.9 minutes but was limited to 43 games last season.
He missed more than two months with a nagging right knee injury before he finally came back in early April. He had initially hoped to return after the All-Star break.
Curry has won four NBA titles with Golden State, most recently in 2022.
"We've been incredibly blessed to experience 17 years of Stephen's artistry and are thrilled that our fans will continue to have the opportunity to watch him perform and write additional chapters to his illustrious story," Dunleavy said.
ESPN first reported Curry's new deal.

articles.content_orig:
When it comes to coach-speak, Brandt Snedeker has kept the transcriptionists busier than the airspace over Medinah this week.
Like a 737 taking off from nearby O’Hare, the Internationals roared into a 7-3 lead Friday at the Presidents Cup, sweeping a foursomes session for the second time in as many editions of this biennial competition that has been dominated by the Americans (13-1-1).
The Americans are suddenly on their back feet, and naturally, the U.S. skipper was pressed for answers:
“They made a ton of putts.”
“You’re going to have sessions like this.”
“Just didn’t quite get the right momentum we wanted.”
“There’s a lot of golf left to play.”
“We’re going to view it as an opportunity.”
Get the idea? Well, here’s a closer look at what went wrong on Friday at Medinah:
1. The Internationals did, in fact, make more putts
It’s easy to blame the Americans’ continued foursomes skid (6-24 in the format since the start of the 2023 Ryder Cup) on an inability to make more putts than their opponents.
“I feel like we had the right matchups, we felt like,” Snedeker said, “and some days the ball just doesn’t want to go in.”
But Snedeker, one of the best putters of the 21st century, has a valid point.
Min Woo Lee and Ryan Fox basically couldn’t miss, rolling in five birdie putts from outside of 10 feet in a 1-up victory over Wyndham Clark and Collin Morikawa.
Same for Tom Kim and Si Woo Kim.
Adam Scott and Christiaan Bezuidenhout dropped some bombs.
Sungjae Im wasn’t even on the green when he hooped a couple putts.
When the dust settled, eight of the nine worst putters in terms of strokes gained were American. The only exception was Corey Conners, who has made a career out of cashing checks without cashing putts.
Overall, the Internationals gained over six strokes on their opponent with the flatstick.
“Seems like everyone had a few things go their way,” Scott said. “This is what can happen.”
MEDINAH, IL - SEPTEMBER 25: Cameron Young of the United States reacts to a missed putt on No. 15 during the Friday Foursomes session of the Presidents Cup, September 25, 2026, at Medinah Country Club in Medinah, Illinois. (Photo by Matthew Maxey/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images)
Icon Sportswire via Getty Images
2. The Americans got throttled on the non-par-4s
The U.S. combined to win just a dozen holes on Friday, with all but one of those wins coming on par-4s.
Compared to the Internationals, the Americans were abysmal on the par-5s and par-3s.
In terms of holes won, the Internationals boasted a 6-0 advantage on the three-shotters, while outscoring the home side on those two holes, Nos. 3 and 6, 9 under to 3 under.
On the four par-3s, the Internationals outscored their counterparts 5-1 while playing those holes in a collective 4 under, three strokes better than the U.S. players.
“I thought the golf course firmed up a ton today,” Snedeker said. “The ball was bouncing around a lot. The greens were pretty difficult. Chipping is very difficult for these guys around there. Probably a totally different golf course than we saw last week when we got here.”
Added Geoff Ogilvy, the International captain: “It’s pretty satisfying you can have that much rain in the week leading up and we can be playing a pretty firm, fast golf course three days later. Yeah, like Brandt said, it asks a lot of questions. It’s probably tougher than I would have expected.”
3. Snedeker walks into punch
With his team enjoying the early lead on Thursday night, Snedeker was asked if his game plan would change at all based on what transpired in the first session. The U.S. skipper vowed that the Americans were trusting their process, sharing a boxing analogy in the process.
“Everybody has a plan until they get punched in the mouth,” Snedeker said. “Mike Tyson said that famously. We had a really good plan coming in, and we’re still sticking to it.”
But as it turned out, Snedeker might’ve walked into the punch.
Snedeker’s comments came just minutes after he sent Chris Gotterup to his corner following a poor fourball showing. Gotterup appeared set to pair with Cameron Young in foursomes, but instead, Young was thrown on the board with the hot-handed Justin Thomas in the fourth match opposite Scott and Bezuidenhout.
Thomas was 10-0-2 in team play for his Presidents Cup career entering Friday, but his form coming into these matches didn’t exactly align with his past credentials. Any momentum he acquired alongside rookie Jackson Koivun on Thursday dissipated quickly; Thomas lost almost two-and-a-half shots with the putter and finished the day as the only one of 20 players who lost more than four strokes overall.
Afterward, Snedeker contradicted his statements from the previous night, revealing that he made the decision to ride Thomas and pair him with Young despite Thomas and Young being the only one of Friday’s 10 partnerships who didn’t play a single practice round together this week.
“We felt like Justin and Cam had played so well the first day, it was going to be kind of hard to keep them off the golf course,” Snedeker said. “That’s one of the things as captain you look back on maybe when this thing is all over with, it might not have been the right decision, but it seemed like the right decision at the time.”
Can Coach Sneds make the right adjustments this time? With one fewer fourball match on Saturday morning, three American pairs will stay intact, though Xander Schauffele and Patrick Cantlay will be benched as their fourball partners on Thursday, Young and Gotterup, finally team up.
As he and his players head into the Presidents Cup’s proverbial first intermission (in honor of Conners and Nick Taylor, we’re talking hockey), Snedeker declined to share what motivational tools he may use to, borrowing some words from a reporter’s question, “fire the guys up.”
“That stays in the team room,” Snedeker said.
But Snedeker’s parting message to the media was this: “These guys care so much. These guys love being on these teams. They love playing for their country. They love playing for each other. I love teams like that. I think the American people should be damn proud of those 12 guys. … I’m going to keep saying this until I’m blue in the face: These guys are competitive. They don’t like losing anything. They certainly don’t like where we are right now.
“But we’re one-third of the way through this. There’s a helluva lot of golf in front of us, and I’m telling you, these guys are going to come out firing tomorrow.”
It’s unclear whether Snedeker will continue to wear the Chicago Bears hat he’s been donning for much of the week. (The Bears haven’t won a Super Bowl since 1986, Sneds!)
What is clear: The Americans are no longer the prohibitive favorites; in fact, the U.S. enters Saturday as a slight dog.
